q: What most affects concrete strength?
n: The water–cement ratio most affects concrete strength. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (Abrams' law).

q: What is the size of a standard slump cone?
o: 350 mm high, 100 mm top, 200 mm base
300 mm high, 100 mm top, 200 mm base
250 mm high, 75 mm top, 150 mm base
400 mm high, 150 mm top, 250 mm base
n: The standard slump cone is 300 mm high, 100 mm across the top and 200 mm across the base. Source: ASTM C143.

q: What is the maximum allowable slump for vertical concrete elements such as columns and walls?
n: Columns and walls usually allow up to about 100 mm slump. Source: ACI 211.1 (recommended slumps); DPWH Item 405.

q: What is not included in the computation of reinforced concrete load?
n: The reinforced concrete load includes the structure itself (slabs, beams, columns). Floor finishes are a separate superimposed dead load. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 2 (dead loads).

q: Why is concrete cover provided over rebars?
n: Concrete cover over rebars mainly prevents corrosion (rust) and gives fire protection. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 420.6.1.

q: Which admixture delays setting and slows hydration?
n: A retarder delays setting and slows hydration, which helps in hot weather or long hauls. Source: ASTM C494 (Type B); PCA.

q: What is the formula for the modulus of elasticity of normal-weight concrete, in MPa?
n: For normal-weight concrete, NSCP gives the modulus of elasticity as Ec = 4,700 √f'c (MPa). Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 419.2.2.1.

q: Which admixture lets concrete use less water?
n: A plasticizer (water reducer) lets concrete reach the same workability with less water, which raises strength. Source: ASTM C494 (Type A/F); PCA.

q: What is the minimum cover for a column footing cast on soil?
n: Footings cast against and permanently exposed to earth need 75 mm cover. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1.

q: What is the minimum clearance from the bottom of reinforcement bars to the bottom of a beam exposed to the atmosphere?
n: Concrete exposed to weather needs 40 mm cover for 16 mm bars and smaller (50 mm for 20–36 mm bars). Interior beams need 40 mm to the primary bars and stirrups. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1.

q: What is the minimum concrete cover for pipes or conduits exposed to earth or weather?
n: Embedded pipes and conduits need at least 40 mm cover where the concrete is exposed to earth or weather, and 20 mm where it is not. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 420.7 (embedments); ACI 318-14 Sec. 20.7.

q: What is the required cover for a suspended slab not exposed to weather?
n: Slabs not exposed to weather or ground need 20 mm cover for bars 36 mm and smaller. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1.

q: What is the minimum concrete cover for a cast-in-place slab exposed to weather and reinforced with 16 mm bars or smaller?
n: Cast-in-place concrete exposed to weather, with 16 mm bars or smaller, needs 40 mm cover. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1.

q: What is the required concrete cover for walls?
n: Walls not exposed to weather or ground need 20 mm cover for bars 36 mm and smaller. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1.

q: What is the required cover for interior beams?
n: Beams not exposed to weather need 40 mm cover to the primary reinforcement, ties and stirrups. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1.

q: Why does required cover increase with exposure?
o: To protect bars from moisture and corrosion
n: More exposure to moisture and aggressive agents calls for more cover, to protect the bars from corrosion. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 420.6.1; ACI 201.2R.

q: Which is the most expensive concrete in terms of curing time?
n: The longer concrete must be cured before use, the more time and cost it adds. Of the choices, 30 days is the longest and most expensive curing schedule. Source: ACI 308R (Guide to Curing Concrete).

q: How many days before you can walk on a freshly poured concrete slab?
n: Light foot traffic is usually possible after about 1–2 days, once the slab has set and gained early strength. Source: ACI 302.1R; PCA.

q: What is the most common curing method locally?
n: The most common local curing method is wet curing by sprinkling or spraying water (ponding on slabs). Source: ACI 308R; DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.

q: After how many days is concrete taken to reach its design strength?
n: Concrete is taken to reach its specified design strength (f'c) at 28 days. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.12; ASTM C39.

q: What is the fastest curing time for a concrete mix to gain sufficient early strength?
n: By about 7 days concrete reaches roughly 65–70% of its 28-day strength, usually enough early strength for form removal or early checks. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: What paste of cement, sand and water is laid between bricks or blocks?
n: Mortar is the paste of cement, sand and water laid between bricks or blocks. Mortar bonds the units, levels them and seals the joints against water. Source: ASTM C270.

q: What is the typical cement-to-sand ratio for plastering?
n: A cement-to-sand ratio of about 1:3 is common for plastering. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (plastering tables).

q: What is a common mix ratio for mortar?
n: Masonry mortar is commonly about 1:3 cement to sand (Class B mortar in Fajardo is 1:3). Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 2-1.

q: What happens to fresh concrete in beams and columns if it isn't vibrated?
n: Without vibration, air pockets and voids remain in fresh concrete, leaving honeycombing in beams and columns. Source: ACI 309R (Guide for Consolidation of Concrete).

q: For a10m? concrete slab using a Class A mix, how many bags of cement are required?
n: Class A uses 9.0 bags of 40 kg cement per m³, so a 10 m³ slab needs 10 × 9.0 = 90 bags. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: Which of the following is a Portland cement supplier?
n: Republic Cement is a Philippine Portland cement manufacturer and supplier. Source: Republic Cement & Building Materials (official site).

q: Which of the following is a local brand of Portland cement?
n: Republic Cement is a local Philippine brand of Portland cement. Source: Republic Cement & Building Materials (official site).

q: Which of these is NOT a cement brand?
n: "Portland" is a type of cement (ASTM C150), not a brand. Holcim, Republic and Rizal are brands. Source: ASTM C150; manufacturers' sites.

q: Which company supplies load-bearing concrete hollow blocks (CHB)?
n: Jackbilt is a Philippine manufacturer of load-bearing concrete hollow blocks and precast products. Source: Jackbilt Industries (official site).

q: What is the design live load at the ground floor in kg/m??
n: The NBC sets the first-floor (ground) live load of dwellings at no less than 200 kg/m². Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VII, Sec. 708.

q: What is the design live load at the second floor in kg/m??
n: The second-floor live load of dwellings is no less than 150 kg/m². Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VII, Sec. 708.

q: What is the minimum wind load in kg/m? for vertical roof projections?
n: The wind load for dwelling roofs shall be at least 120 kg/m² on the vertical projection. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VII, Sec. 708.

q: What is the minimum curing time for a concrete cylinder before performing a compressive strength test?
n: Cylinders are commonly first tested at 7 days, the earliest standard check of strength gain. The acceptance test is at 28 days. Source: ASTM C39; ASTM C31.

q: What is the main reason why concrete cracks?
o: Too much water in the water to cement ratio mix
Steel rebars are not properly tied together
Lack of control joints in the concrete slab to allow movement
Insufficient concrete spreading during concrete pouring
n: Excess water (a high water–cement ratio) increases shrinkage and lowers strength, the most common cause of concrete cracking. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures; ACI 224R.

q: What is the best way to cure a slab so it keeps gaining strength?
o: Leave the forms for two weeks
Keep it wet with regular water curing
n: Keeping a slab continuously wet with regular water curing lets it keep hydrating and gaining strength. Source: ACI 308R.

q: What are control joints in a slab on grade for?
o: Making cracks form along planned straight lines
n: Control joints create weakened planes, so shrinkage cracks form along planned straight lines. Source: ACI 224.3R; ACI 302.1R.
